title: Pros & Cons Of Investing In Mutual Funds In A Minor’s Name
summary: How a mutual fund folio in a child's name works, the documents, what changes at 18, how section 99 adds the gains to a parent's income, and the pros and cons.
body_markdown:
Yes. A parent or a court-appointed guardian can invest in a mutual fund in a child's name. The child is the only holder of the account. The guardian runs it until the child turns 18. Money from selling units goes only to the child's own bank account. A child under 18 is a minor, and the guardian is the adult who acts for the child.


The catch is tax. While the child is a minor, gains in the folio (your account with one fund house) are added to a parent's income. So the folio sets money apart, but it saves no tax in those years. This page covers how the folio works, the papers, what happens at 18, the tax, and the pros and cons.


## Can you invest in mutual funds in your child's name?


Yes, through a guardian. Fund houses accept two kinds: a natural guardian, meaning the child's father or mother, or a guardian appointed by a court. This is how one fund house's rule book puts it, citing guidelines from AMFI, the mutual fund industry body.


A guardian can invest in a minor's name on Koshex; the guardian uses the app and makes the decisions.


## How does a mutual fund folio in a child's name work?


The child is the first and only holder, and the guardian operates the folio on the child's behalf. The same fund house document says a minor's folio can have no joint holders and no nominees.


How money goes in and out:


- **Paying in.** SEBI's rules accept payment from the bank account of the minor, a parent or the legal guardian. A joint account of the minor with a parent or guardian also works. That fund house refuses third-party payments except in listed cases, and this is one of them.
- **Taking money out.** Under SEBI's rules, when units are sold (redeemed), the money goes only to the minor's verified bank account.
- **SIPs.** A[SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) is a fixed amount invested at regular intervals, usually monthly. You can run one in a child's folio, until the child turns 18.


Can a minor redeem on their own? No. The guardian operates the folio until the child turns 18, and the money still goes to the child's account.


## What documents do you need?


Fund houses ask for proof of the child's age and proof of your relationship to the child. They also ask for your own KYC and PAN (Permanent Account Number). KYC is the identity check investors complete before investing. One fund house's document asks for a date-of-birth proof such as a birth certificate, a school leaving certificate or a passport.


For the relationship, SEBI's KYC answers say a document proving it must be provided. Fund houses ask a court-appointed guardian for the court order.


Does your child need a PAN? No. A child with no taxable income may quote a parent's or guardian's PAN instead (rule 159(2)(a) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026). Fund houses still ask for the guardian's PAN and KYC in every case. One fund house's document says the guardian's PAN copy is mandatory whether or not the child has a PAN.


For how KYC itself works, read our[mutual fund KYC guide](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-kyc) .


## What happens when your child turns 18?


From the 18th birthday you can no longer operate the folio. SEBI's rules say the minor must then give all KYC details and updated bank account details. That includes a cancelled original cheque leaf of the new account. No further transactions are allowed until the status changes from minor to major.


In practice:


- One fund house's document says it writes to the child asking for the change of status, along with the documents it prescribes.
- SIPs and other automatic instructions on the folio are suspended until the status is changed. No new investment is accepted either.
- Once the child completes their own KYC and registers their own bank account, the folio is theirs.


The same fund house's document says a parent, guardian or sibling can then be added as a joint holder. Before 18, fund houses do not accept a nomination on a folio held in a child's name. Once the folio is in the child's own name, they can add nominees. For how nomination works in general, see[mutual fund nomination](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-nomination) .


## How are gains in a child's folio taxed?


While your child is under 18, income from their mutual funds, including capital gains, is added to one parent's income, as set out below. A capital gain is the profit you make when you sell units for more than you paid. Adding a child's income to a parent's is called clubbing. It comes from section 99 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (the old section 64(1A)).


- If the parents are married, the income goes to the parent whose total income is higher. If they are not married to each other, it goes to the parent who maintains the child during the tax year.
- The first ₹1,500 a year per child is exempt (Schedule III, the old section 10(32)).
- Income from the child's own work, or from a skill or talent the child uses, is not added. Nor is the income of a child with a disability as defined in the tax law.
- Once the child turns 18, income arising after that is the child's own. Units sold before the 18th birthday are clubbed. Units sold after it are taxed in the child's hands.


Here is an example with assumed numbers, for illustration only. A 9-year-old's folio holds equity-oriented fund units (funds that keep at least 65% of their money in shares of Indian listed companies) bought over 12 months ago. Securities transaction tax (STT) was paid on them. In 2026-27 the guardian redeems them, with an assumed long-term gain of ₹60,000. The parents are married. The father has the higher income and ₹1,00,000 of long-term equity fund gains of his own that year.


- ₹1,500 is exempt, so ₹58,500 is added to the father's income.
- His long-term equity gains become ₹1,58,500.
- Long-term gains on equity-oriented funds are taxed at 12.5% on the amount above ₹1,25,000 in a tax year. That is 12.5% of ₹33,500, which is ₹4,187.50. With 4% cess (an extra 4% charge on the tax), the tax is ₹4,355 (resident individual, tax year 2026-27, total income not above ₹50 lakh).


Note that the ₹1,25,000 allowance is the father's, once a year. The child's clubbed gain uses part of it. No tax is deducted at source (TDS) on a resident's redemption, and the money still goes to the child's account. Had the units been sold after the 18th birthday, the gain would be the child's, with the child's own ₹1,25,000 allowance.


Income from units you gift to your spouse or your son's wife is also added to yours; see[how to gift mutual fund units](https://koshex.com/blog/gift-mutual-fund-units) .


## What are the pros and cons of a mutual fund in a child's name?


The main pro and the main con are the same fact: the money becomes the child's.


Pros Cons


Money is set apart, and redemption money is paid only to the child's own account. Control passes at 18. The guardian can no longer operate the folio.


SIPs are possible while the child is a minor. The folio freezes at 18 until the child changes its status and gives their own KYC and bank details.


The child can watch it grow over the years. No joint holder or nominee while the child is a minor, as fund houses set it up.


After 18, gains are taxed as the child's own income. No tax saving while the child is a minor, because income is added to a parent's.


## Should you invest in your child's name or set aside money in your own?


Either can work, and the choice turns on a few factors, not a rule. Look at who should control the money at 18. A child's folio passes to the child at 18. A folio in your own name stays in your name.


Look at whether you might need the money yourself. Money in the child's folio can be redeemed only into the child's account. Tax falls on a parent either way until the child turns 18, because the child's income is added to a parent's. A folio in your own name can also carry a nominee, which a minor's folio cannot (see[mutual fund nomination](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-nomination) ).
